title: README
content:
AI-generated images have become increasingly common thanks to models like DALL-E, Midjourney, and Stable Diffusion, which can create pictures that look very realistic. Because these images can be so convincing, it’s important to have ways to tell whether an image was created by a human or by AI. This is what AI-generated image detection is all about. The goal is to develop methods that can identify images made by these generative models, which helps in areas like verifying authenticity and preventing misinformation.

To understand how this detection works, it helps to start with some basics about how images and AI models function. Images are made up of pixels arranged in patterns, and AI models that generate images learn to create these patterns in ways that mimic real photos. However, even the best AI-generated images often have subtle differences from real ones, and these differences can be detected using specialized techniques.

One common approach to detecting AI-generated images uses deep learning, specifically convolutional neural networks, or CNNs. CNNs are a type of neural network designed to work with images. They scan images with filters that pick up on patterns like edges, textures, and shapes. By training a CNN on a dataset of real and AI-generated images, the network learns to recognize the subtle clues that distinguish the two. This method works well when you know which AI model created the images because the CNN can learn the specific patterns associated with that model.

Sometimes, though, you might encounter images generated by AI models you haven’t seen before. In these cases, deep learning methods trained on known models might not perform well. That’s where statistical methods come in. Instead of relying on learned patterns, statistical approaches analyze the image’s properties to find anomalies—unusual patterns or inconsistencies that don’t typically appear in natural images. These anomalies can be clues that the image was artificially generated, even if the exact AI model is unknown.

Another important concept in this field is frequency domain analysis. Instead of looking at images just as pixels, this method transforms the image data to examine how pixel values change across the image in terms of frequency. AI-generated images often have unique frequency patterns that are hard to spot by just looking at the image but become clear when analyzed this way.

Because training deep learning models from scratch can require a lot of data and computing power, a technique called transfer learning is often used. This means starting with a model that’s already been trained on a large, general image dataset and then fine-tuning it for the specific task of detecting AI-generated images. This approach saves time and resources and usually improves performance, especially when you don’t have a huge dataset of labeled images.

To make models more robust, data augmentation is commonly applied. This involves creating variations of the training images by rotating, flipping, or changing colors slightly. These variations help the model learn to recognize AI-generated images under different conditions and reduce the chance that it will only work well on the exact images it was trained on.

When training and evaluating these models, it’s important to use the right metrics. Precision tells you how many of the images the model flagged as AI-generated actually are AI-generated. Recall tells you how many of the AI-generated images the model successfully detected. The F1-score balances these two, and ROC curves help visualize the trade-off between detecting true positives and avoiding false alarms. These metrics help you understand how well your detection method is working.

Before diving into this topic, it’s helpful to have some basic skills. Knowing Python programming is important because the code examples and implementations use it. Understanding basic machine learning concepts like supervised learning and how to split data into training and validation sets will also make it easier to follow. Familiarity with PyTorch, a popular deep learning library, is useful but not strictly necessary. Finally, some basic knowledge of image processing—like what pixels and color channels are—will help you understand how images are handled in these methods.

The study materials for this topic are organized to guide you step-by-step. You start by learning about the problem and the overall approach, then move on to deep learning methods for known AI models, followed by statistical methods for unknown models. Along the way, you’ll explore key concepts and best practices, and finally, you’ll get hands-on experience with code notebooks that let you try out the techniques yourself.

This structured approach helps you build a solid understanding, combining theory with practical skills. It’s designed so that even if you’re not an expert, you can follow along and gradually develop the ability to detect AI-generated images effectively. If you’re interested in this area, working through these materials and practicing with the code will give you a good foundation to build on.

title: external_resources
content:
Detecting images created by artificial intelligence has become an important challenge as AI-generated visuals become more common and harder to distinguish from real photos. One effective way to approach this problem is by combining two methods: a deep learning technique that looks at the image’s frequency patterns, and a statistical method that spots unusual features that don’t fit known patterns. The deep learning part is called the FIRE method, which stands for Frequency-guided Reconstruction Error. It works by analyzing the image in the frequency domain, which means it looks at how different frequency components—like the fine details and textures—are arranged. AI-generated images often have subtle artifacts or inconsistencies in these frequency patterns because of how the models create images, especially diffusion models. By reconstructing the image focusing on these frequency details and measuring how much error there is in the reconstruction, the FIRE method can tell if an image is likely AI-generated.

To build and test this kind of detector, researchers rely on large datasets that contain both real and AI-generated images. One of the most important datasets is called GenImage, which has over a million pairs of images from various AI generators and real sources. This dataset helps train models like FIRE and also tests how well they work on images from different AI systems, which is important because new AI generators keep appearing. The dataset covers a wide range of image types and styles, making it a solid benchmark for evaluating detection methods.

The idea of using frequency analysis to detect AI images isn’t new. Earlier research showed that GAN-generated images, for example, leave telltale signs in the frequency domain because of the way they upsample images during generation. These findings inspired the FIRE method and similar approaches that focus on frequency features rather than just pixel-level details. More recent work has emphasized that focusing on high-frequency components—the fine details and edges—helps detectors generalize better to new AI models they haven’t seen before.

Alongside the deep learning approach, there’s also a statistical angle that treats AI-generated images as anomalies. This means the detector looks for images that don’t fit the normal patterns of real images, even if the AI model that created them is unknown. This anomaly detection complements the deep learning method by catching images from new or less common AI generators.

To implement these methods, several tools and libraries are essential. OpenCV is widely used for image processing and frequency domain operations like Fourier transforms, which are key to analyzing frequency components. Albumentations helps with data augmentation, which means creating variations of training images to make the model more robust. PyTorch and Torchvision provide the deep learning framework and pre-built models that make it easier to build and train the FIRE CNN architecture.

Beyond the core methods and datasets, the field is evolving with new research exploring different angles. Some studies use vision-language models like CLIP, which combine image and text understanding, to improve detection across many types of AI-generated images. Others focus on removing biases in training data to make detectors more reliable. There’s also growing interest in combining multiple signals—like image content, metadata, and text—to improve detection accuracy.

In practice, there are commercial and open-source tools available for AI image detection, such as Hive Moderation and StableGuard, which use machine learning models to identify AI-generated content. These tools are useful for comparison and real-world applications.

Evaluating detection methods involves several metrics, including accuracy, precision, recall, and the area under the ROC curve. It’s also important to test how well detectors perform on images from AI generators they weren’t trained on, which shows how well they generalize.

Looking ahead, the main challenges include improving detection for new and unseen AI models, making detection fast enough for real-time use, and making models more resistant to attempts to fool them. Researchers are also working on making detection results easier to understand, so users know why an image was flagged.

Overall, detecting AI-generated images is a complex problem that benefits from combining frequency-based deep learning with statistical anomaly detection. Using large, diverse datasets and robust tools helps build detectors that can keep up with the fast pace of AI image generation technology.

title: study_guide_concepts
content:
Today, we’re going to talk about how deep learning helps us detect whether an image is real or generated by AI, and the key ideas behind making that work. At the core, this is a binary classification problem, which means the model has to decide between two options: is the image real or AI-generated? The model looks at an image and outputs a number that represents how confident it is that the image is AI-generated. We then convert this number into a probability between zero and one, and if it’s above a certain threshold, usually 0.5, we say the image is AI-generated. To train the model, we use a loss function that measures how far off the model’s predictions are from the true labels, helping it improve over time.

The models we use for images are called convolutional neural networks, or CNNs. These networks are designed to work with images by looking at small patches and learning to recognize patterns like edges, textures, and shapes. They do this through layers that apply filters across the image, capturing important features automatically. After these convolutional layers, the network uses pooling to reduce the size of the data while keeping the important information, which helps the model focus on what really matters regardless of where it appears in the image. Finally, fully connected layers take all these learned features and make the final decision about the image’s class.

Often, instead of training a model from scratch, we use transfer learning. This means we start with a model that’s already been trained on a large dataset of images, like ImageNet, which contains millions of pictures. The early layers of this pretrained model have learned to detect very general features like edges and textures, which are useful for many tasks. We keep those layers and only retrain the last part of the model to specialize it for our specific task of detecting AI-generated images. This approach saves time, requires less data, and usually leads to better results.

Another important concept is looking at images not just as pixels but in terms of their frequency content. The Fast Fourier Transform, or FFT, is a tool that changes an image from the spatial domain, where we see pixels, to the frequency domain, where we see patterns of repetition and texture at different scales. Real images and AI-generated images often have different frequency signatures. For example, AI images might have smoother high-frequency details or missing mid-range patterns that real images naturally have. By analyzing these frequency patterns, we can find clues that help us tell real and fake images apart.

We can also apply band-pass filters in the frequency domain to focus on specific ranges of frequencies. This means we keep only certain frequencies and remove others, which can help reduce noise or highlight features that are important for detecting AI artifacts. For instance, filtering out very high or very low frequencies can make it easier to spot unnatural patterns that AI models tend to produce.

Training these models efficiently requires some tricks. One is gradient accumulation, which lets us simulate training with larger batches even if our hardware can’t handle them all at once. We do this by splitting a large batch into smaller parts, calculating gradients for each, and only updating the model after accumulating enough of these smaller steps. This helps stabilize training and manage memory better. Another technique is mixed precision training, which uses lower-precision numbers for some calculations to speed up training and reduce memory use without hurting accuracy. Adjusting the learning rate during training is also important. Instead of keeping it constant, we reduce it when the model stops improving, or follow schedules that gradually lower it, helping the model settle into a better solution.

Handling data properly is just as important as the model itself. We use custom dataset classes to load images and labels on demand, which saves memory because we don’t load everything at once. Data loaders then take care of batching, shuffling, and loading data in parallel, making training faster and more efficient. To make the model more robust, we apply image augmentations—random changes like flipping, adjusting brightness, or adding noise. These augmentations help the model learn to recognize images even when they vary in small ways.

Statistical methods like kernel density estimation help us understand the distribution of data or model outputs by smoothing out noisy histograms. This can reveal where the data tends to cluster or peak. Percentiles and confidence intervals give us a way to summarize data ranges and understand the uncertainty in our measurements.

When evaluating models, we look at several metrics. Accuracy tells us the overall correctness, but it can be misleading if classes are imbalanced. Precision and recall give us more insight into how well the model identifies positives without too many false alarms or misses. The F1 score balances precision and recall, and the area under the ROC curve shows how well the model separates the two classes across different thresholds.

Good coding practices help keep projects manageable. Separating data loading, model building, training, and evaluation into different parts makes the code easier to understand and maintain. Logging progress and saving checkpoints lets us track training and recover from interruptions. Debugging involves checking that data shapes and types are correct, ensuring the loss decreases, and monitoring gradients to catch problems early. Performance can be improved by using multiple data loading workers, pinning memory for faster GPU transfers, and profiling code to find bottlenecks.

Common pitfalls include data leaks, where test data accidentally ends up in training, leading to overly optimistic results. Overfitting happens when the model learns the training data too well but fails to generalize, which we can combat with validation sets, early stopping, regularization, and augmentation. Memory issues can be managed by reducing batch size, using gradient accumulation, or choosing smaller models.

Finally, there are advanced topics like multi-task learning, where one model learns several related tasks at once, ensemble methods that combine multiple models for better accuracy, domain adaptation to transfer knowledge between different types of data, and few-shot learning, which aims to learn from very few examples. These areas are more complex but offer exciting possibilities for improving AI image detection.

That covers the main ideas behind detecting AI-generated images using deep learning, frequency analysis, and smart training and data handling techniques. Understanding these concepts gives you a solid foundation to explore this field further.

title: study_guide_intro
content:
Detecting AI-generated images is becoming an important challenge as AI models get better at creating pictures that look real. These images can be so convincing that it’s hard for people to tell if they were made by a computer or a camera. The goal here is to build a system that can automatically decide whether an image is real or generated by AI. This is a binary classification problem, meaning the system labels each image as either real or AI-generated.

The problem has two parts. First, we want to detect images made by AI models we already know about and have examples of. This is a typical supervised learning task because we have labeled data showing both real and AI-generated images from these known models. Second, we want to detect images from AI models we haven’t seen before. This is harder because we don’t have training examples for these unknown models. Instead, we treat this as an anomaly detection problem, where we look for images that don’t fit the usual patterns of real images.

Why does this matter? As AI-generated images become more common, they can be used to spread misinformation or create fake content that looks real. Being able to detect these images helps maintain trust in what we see online and supports efforts to moderate harmful content. It also shows how combining different machine learning methods can lead to better results.

The approach to solving this problem has two stages. In the first stage, for known AI models, we use deep learning. We train a neural network to recognize subtle clues and patterns that these AI models leave behind. Deep learning works well here because it can find complex features in images that humans might miss. The model looks at both the arrangement of pixels and patterns in the image’s frequency domain, which means it analyzes how pixel values change across the image in ways that reveal AI generation.

In the second stage, for unknown AI models, we can’t rely on having seen examples before. Instead, we use statistical methods to find images that don’t match the normal patterns of real images. Real photos tend to follow certain statistical rules in their colors and textures, even though they can be very diverse. AI-generated images often break these rules in subtle ways. By establishing what “normal” looks like from real images, we can flag images that fall outside these expected patterns.

Before working on this, it helps to have some background knowledge. You should be comfortable with basic Python programming, including how to write functions and use loops. Understanding PyTorch is important because it’s the main tool for building and training neural networks here. You should know what tensors are, how automatic differentiation works, and how to use neural network modules. It’s also useful to understand how convolutional neural networks work, since they are the backbone of image analysis. Basic image processing knowledge, like how RGB channels work and what pixel values mean, is necessary. Finally, some understanding of statistics, like distributions and percentiles, will help with the anomaly detection part.

Several libraries make this work easier. PyTorch is the main deep learning framework, and Torchvision builds on it with tools specific to images, like pretrained models and transformations. Albumentations helps with image augmentation, which means creating variations of images to improve training. OpenCV is useful for image processing tasks like computing histograms. NumPy and Pandas handle numerical data and tabular data, respectively. Scikit-learn provides tools for evaluating models, like calculating accuracy and other metrics.

By the end of this study, you’ll learn how to build CNNs that combine spatial and frequency features to better detect AI-generated images. You’ll understand how to create efficient data loading pipelines that handle large datasets without running out of memory. You’ll also learn advanced training techniques like gradient accumulation, which lets you train bigger models even with limited hardware, and mixed precision training, which speeds up training. On the statistical side, you’ll learn how to use methods like kernel density estimation and percentile thresholds to spot anomalies. Finally, you’ll see how combining deep learning and statistical methods can create a more reliable detection system. Along the way, you’ll pick up skills in debugging and optimizing your models and training pipelines.

The project is organized into several parts. The introduction explains the problem and approach. One part focuses on detecting known AI-generated images using deep learning. Another part covers detecting unknown AI-generated images using statistical analysis. There’s also a section that explains key concepts and implementation details.

Overall, this work shows how to tackle a real-world problem by combining different machine learning techniques. It prepares you to handle similar challenges in computer vision and anomaly detection, where you need to identify subtle differences in complex data.

title: study_guide_part1
content:
Today, we’re going to talk about how to detect images created by AI models, specifically when we know which AI model generated them. Even though AI-generated images can look very realistic, they often have subtle differences from real photos that humans can’t easily see. These differences show up as patterns or artifacts in the image, and by training a neural network on examples of both real and AI-generated images, we can teach it to spot those differences.

The approach we use is a type of supervised learning, meaning the model learns from labeled examples—images tagged as either real or AI-generated. What makes this method interesting is that it doesn’t just look at the image in the usual way, by analyzing pixels and shapes, but also examines the image in the frequency domain. This means it looks at how different frequencies—think of them as different levels of detail or texture—are distributed across the image. Real photos and AI images tend to have different frequency patterns, so combining spatial and frequency information gives the model a better chance to tell them apart.

The model we focus on is a simplified version of something called the FIRE model. It has two main parts: one that extracts traditional spatial features using a convolutional neural network, and another that extracts frequency features by applying a filter in the frequency domain. The frequency filter works by transforming the image using a mathematical tool called the Fourier transform, which breaks down the image into its frequency components. Then it applies a band-pass filter to focus on mid-range frequencies, which often carry the most useful clues for distinguishing AI images. After filtering, it converts the data back to a form the neural network can use.

Once we have both the original image and the frequency-filtered version, the model combines them by feeding all six channels—three from the original RGB image and three from the frequency features—into a modified ResNet18 network. This network was originally trained on a large dataset of real images, so it already knows how to extract useful features. To handle the extra frequency channels, the first layer of the network is adjusted to accept six channels instead of three, and the weights for the new channels are initialized by copying the weights from the original RGB channels. This gives the frequency features a good starting point instead of random initialization.

Before training, we prepare the data carefully. Instead of loading all images into memory, which would be inefficient, we store file paths and load images only when needed during training. This makes it possible to work with large datasets without running out of memory. We also use a subset of images to speed up experimentation, but in practice, more data usually helps. Labels are encoded simply: zero for real images and one for AI-generated ones.

Data augmentation plays a big role in making the model robust. By applying random transformations like slight blurring, compression, flipping, cropping, and color changes, we create many different versions of the same image. This prevents the model from memorizing specific details and helps it generalize better to new images. We use weaker augmentations during validation to keep the images close to their original form, and stronger augmentations during training to expose the model to a wider variety of examples.

Training the model involves some practical techniques to make the process efficient and stable. For example, gradient accumulation allows us to simulate larger batch sizes by accumulating gradients over several smaller batches before updating the model’s weights. Mixed precision training speeds things up and reduces memory use by using lower-precision numbers where possible. We also adjust the learning rate during training, lowering it when the model’s performance on validation data stops improving.

The loss function used combines a sigmoid activation with binary cross-entropy, which is more stable than applying them separately. The optimizer is Adam, which adapts the learning rate for each parameter, helping the model converge faster.

To evaluate how well the model works, we look at several metrics. Accuracy tells us the overall percentage of correct predictions. The area under the ROC curve, or AUC, measures how well the model ranks AI-generated images higher than real ones. The F1 score balances precision and recall, which are important when false positives and false negatives have different consequences. Precision measures how many predicted AI images are actually AI-generated, and recall measures how many actual AI images the model correctly identifies.

When using the model for inference, we switch it to evaluation mode to disable certain training behaviors and avoid calculating gradients, which saves resources. The model outputs raw scores, which we convert to probabilities using a sigmoid function. These probabilities can then be thresholded to make final predictions.

Some common questions come up with this approach. For example, why combine spatial and frequency features? The answer is that frequency analysis reveals patterns that spatial CNNs might miss, especially since AI-generated images often have distinct frequency signatures. Why use gradient accumulation? It lets us train with effectively larger batch sizes without needing more GPU memory. And why use the combined loss function? Because it’s more numerically stable and helps the model learn better.

To deepen your understanding, you can try changing the frequency filter’s parameters to see how different frequency bands affect performance, experiment with different backbone networks like ResNet50 or EfficientNet, test various augmentation strategies, or implement early stopping based on validation performance to avoid overfitting.

Overall, this method shows how combining traditional image analysis with frequency domain insights can improve our ability to detect AI-generated images, even when they look very convincing to the human eye.

title: study_guide_part2
content:
Detecting AI-generated images from models we haven’t seen before is a tricky problem because we can’t rely on training a neural network with examples of those images. Instead, one effective way to approach this is by looking at the statistical properties of images, specifically how colors are distributed. Real photographs, despite their variety, tend to follow consistent patterns in their color distributions. AI-generated images, even from unknown models, often break these natural patterns in ways we can detect.

A useful tool for this is the color histogram, which counts how many pixels in an image fall into different color categories. For color images, we look at the red, green, and blue channels together, creating a three-dimensional histogram. This means we consider combinations of red, green, and blue values simultaneously, rather than looking at each color separately. This approach captures the relationships between colors better, which helps distinguish natural images from artificial ones.

Once we have this histogram, we simplify it by calculating the average count across all color bins. This average gives us a single number that summarizes the overall color distribution of the image. Real images tend to have histogram averages within a certain range, while AI-generated images often fall outside this range.

To detect unknown AI images, we first build a baseline by collecting a large, representative sample of real images and calculating their histogram averages. We then use statistical methods to define what counts as a normal range for these averages. When we analyze new images, we check if their histogram averages fall within this normal range. If they don’t, we flag them as likely AI-generated.

One important detail is that larger images naturally have higher histogram averages because they contain more pixels. This can bias the detection, making larger images more likely to be classified as AI-generated. Interestingly, this bias is used intentionally because AI-generated images might have different size distributions compared to real photos.

In practice, we start by carefully selecting real images to build our baseline, making sure the sample is large and diverse enough to capture natural variation. Then, for each image, we compute the 3D color histogram and calculate its average. Since this can be computationally heavy for thousands of images, we often use parallel processing to speed things up.

After gathering these averages, we analyze their distribution to find the typical range for real images. We use techniques that smooth the data to find the peak and define a confidence interval around it, which helps us decide what counts as normal variation.

When testing new images, we apply the same process and compare their histogram averages to the baseline range. Images outside this range are considered anomalies and flagged as AI-generated.

This method works well alongside traditional deep learning models that detect known AI-generated images. For images where the deep learning model is uncertain, we use this histogram-based anomaly detection as a second step. This combination improves overall detection accuracy.

There are some things to keep in mind. The method assumes that real images have consistent color distribution patterns, which might not always hold if the dataset is biased. Also, the choice of confidence interval affects how sensitive the detection is to anomalies. The approach is fast and doesn’t require retraining for new AI models, making it practical for real-world use.

If you want to explore further, you can try changing the number of bins in the histogram, using different statistical measures like median or standard deviation, or even analyzing each color channel separately. You can also experiment with different confidence levels to see how they affect detection performance.

In summary, by focusing on the statistical properties of color distributions in images, we can detect AI-generated images from unknown models without needing labeled examples. This approach is simple, efficient, and complements existing deep learning methods, helping us keep up with the evolving landscape of AI-generated content.
